title: BioE_Stats_2026_HW3
text:
Assignment: Your task is to use R and Quarto Markdown to write a short report including the tasks listed below. You will work with simulated data that you create, as well as a new dataset studying the mechanical properties of 3D-printed bone scaffolds (scaffold_mechanics.csv). At the beginning of the Quarto file include a data dictionary for each of the variables in the dataset (as best you can tell what they are), and be sure to load all of the packages at the beginning. You will need to use tidyverse tools for data wrangling, ggplot2 for visualization, and the modeling and post-hoc packages introduced in Weeks 4–6.
Due: Submit your work via Canvas by the end of the day (midnight) on Thursday, February 19th. Please submit both the Quarto .qmd file and the resulting html or pdf file. You can work with other members of class, but I expect each of you to construct and run all of the scripts yourself.




A research group in the Knight Campus is developing 3D-printed bone scaffolds using polycaprolactone (PCL). They fabricated 60 scaffolds with varying porosity (percent void volume, ranging from 30–80%) and measured each scaffold’s compressive strength (in MPa) and cell viability (percentage of live cells after 7 days of culture).

Simulate the dataset. Generate 60 observations where porosity is drawn from a uniform distribution between 30 and 80. Generate compressive_strength as a function of porosity with the relationship: \(strength = 45 - 0.4 \times porosity + \epsilon\), where \(\epsilon \sim N(0, 3)\). Generate cell_viability as: \(viability = 40 + 0.5 \times porosity + \epsilon\), where \(\epsilon \sim N(0, 5)\). Combine these into a data frame called scaffold.
Explore the relationships visually. Create two scatter plots — one of compressive strength vs. porosity and one of cell viability vs. porosity. Add a linear regression line to each. Briefly describe what you see.
Calculate Pearson correlations between porosity and each response variable. Test whether each correlation is statistically significant using cor.test(). Interpret the strength and direction of each relationship.
Calculate the Spearman rank correlation for the same two pairs. Compare these values to the Pearson correlations and briefly explain when you would prefer Spearman over Pearson.
Fit a simple linear model of compressive strength as a function of porosity using lm(). Use tidy() and glance() from the broom package to extract the coefficients and model summary. Interpret the slope, intercept, \(R^2\), and p-value in the context of scaffold engineering.
Create a residual plot (residuals vs. fitted values) for your linear model and a Normal Q-Q plot of the residuals. Assess whether the assumptions of linearity, constant variance, and normality appear to be met.





For this exercise, you will continue using the scaffold data from Exercise 3.1, but you will add some problematic observations and explore polynomial regression.

Introduce outliers. Add three observations to your scaffold data frame with the following values. These represent data entry errors or instrument malfunctions:

Observation 61: porosity = 50, compressive_strength = 5, cell_viability = 90
Observation 62: porosity = 45, compressive_strength = 60, cell_viability = 55
Observation 63: porosity = 90, compressive_strength = 15, cell_viability = 85

Refit the linear model of compressive strength vs. porosity using the contaminated dataset. Use autoplot() from ggfortify to generate the four standard diagnostic plots (Residuals vs. Fitted, Normal Q-Q, Scale-Location, and Cook’s Distance). Identify which observations are flagged as problematic and explain why.
Use Cook’s distance to identify influential points. Which observations have Cook’s distance greater than \(4/n\)? Remove them and refit the model. Compare the \(R^2\) and coefficients before and after removal.
Fit a polynomial regression. Using the cleaned dataset (outliers removed), fit a quadratic model of compressive strength as a function of porosity using poly(porosity, 2, raw = TRUE). Use anova() to compare the linear and quadratic models. Is the quadratic term justified?
Visualize both fits. Create a side-by-side plot (using patchwork) showing the linear fit and the quadratic fit on the cleaned data. Include the \(R^2\) value in each plot subtitle.





Use a dataset that you are working with for your term project (or one of the class datasets like Drerio_development_complete.csv or Stickle_RNAseq.tsv).



Pick one continuous response variable and one continuous predictor. Fit a simple linear model, produce diagnostic plots, and interpret the results (slope, \(R^2\), residual patterns).
Write a short paragraph summarizing your findings. What did you learn about your data? Were the model assumptions met? What would you do differently or explore next?

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
DRAFT: Dissimilarity / Distance Formulas







Dissimilarity
Equation




Minkowski
\(\left(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p} \lvert y_{1j} - y_{2j} \rvert^{\lambda}\right)^{1/\lambda}\)


Euclidean (\(\lambda = 2\))
\(\sqrt{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p}(y_{1j} - y_{2j})^2}\)


City block / Manhattan (\(\lambda = 1\))
\(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert y_{1j} - y_{2j}\rvert\)


Canberra
\(\dfrac{1}{p-q}\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p}\dfrac{\lvert y_{1j} - y_{2j}\rvert}{y_{1j} + y_{2j}}\)


Bray–Curtis
\(\dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert y_{1j} - y_{2j}\rvert}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p}(y_{1j} + y_{2j})}\)


Chi-square
\(\sqrt{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p}\dfrac{\left(y_{1j}\dfrac{\sum y_{1j} - y_{2j}}{\sum y_{2j}}\right)^2}{\sum y_j}}\)

Handling Missing Data in Multivariate Analysis



Type
Description
Problem Severity




MCAR

Least problematic

Moderate concern

Most problematic









Three Main Approaches



Deletion — remove observations with missing values (simple but loses information)
Imputation — infer missing values (mean/median or multiple imputation)
Maximum Likelihood / EM — use all available data (most sophisticated)

Why Use MANOVA?

When interested in the relationship of two or more response variables and one or more predictor variables
Tests whether group centroids differ across multiple variables simultaneously
More powerful than running separate univariate ANOVAs when response variables are correlated

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
MANOVA Linear Model
Single Factor MANOVA uses a linear combination of p response variables:

EquationKey Matrices


\[z_{ik} = c_1 y_{i1} + c_2 y_{i2} + c_3 y_{i3} + \ldots + c_p y_{ip}\]



H matrix: Between-groups sums of squares and cross-products
E matrix: Within-groups sums of squares and cross-products
T matrix: Total sums of squares and cross-products
The ratio H/E is decomposed into eigenvalues and eigenvectors

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
MANOVA Assumptions

Multivariate Normality — less critical for Pillai’s trace
Homogeneity of Variance-Covariance — test with Box’s M
Independence of observations
No Multicollinearity among response variables







Outliers


MANOVA is very sensitive to multivariate outliers. Use Mahalanobis distance to detect them.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
Detecting Multivariate Outliers

OutputCode














iris_numeric <- iris[, 1:4]
center <- colMeans(iris_numeric)
cov_matrix <- cov(iris_numeric)
mahal_dist <- mahalanobis(iris_numeric, center, cov_matrix)

plot(mahal_dist, pch = 19, main = "Mahalanobis Distances",
     ylab = "Mahalanobis Distance", xlab = "Observation")
abline(h = qchisq(0.975, df = 4), col = "red", lwd = 2)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
MANOVA Follow-Up Workflow
After a significant MANOVA, determine which variables drive the group differences:

CodeWorkflow Summary



# Step 1: MANOVA
manova_result <- manova(cbind(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width,
                               Petal.Length, Petal.Width) ~ Species,
                         data = iris)
summary(manova_result, test = "Pillai")

# Step 2: Univariate follow-up ANOVAs
summary.aov(manova_result)

# Step 3: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons for each response
library(emmeans)
for (var in c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width",
              "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width")) {
  cat("\n---", var, "---\n")
  fit <- lm(as.formula(paste(var, "~ Species")), data = iris)
  em <- emmeans(fit, pairwise ~ Species, adjust = "bonferroni")
  print(em$contrasts)
}

# Step 4: Effect sizes (eta-squared for each variable)
library(car)
for (var in c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width",
              "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width")) {
  fit <- lm(as.formula(paste(var, "~ Species")), data = iris)
  aov_table <- Anova(fit, type = "II")
  ss_group <- aov_table$`Sum Sq`[1]
  ss_total <- sum(aov_table$`Sum Sq`)
  cat(var, "eta² =", round(ss_group / ss_total, 3), "\n")
}




MANOVA: Test overall multivariate difference → significant?
Univariate ANOVAs: Which response variables differ?
Post-hoc tests: Which groups differ on each variable?
Effect sizes: How large are the differences?
DFA/LDA: Which combinations of variables best discriminate groups?

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
LDA Cross-Validation for Honest Accuracy
Training and testing on the same data gives overly optimistic accuracy estimates. Use leave-one-out CV:

CodeClassifier Comparison



library(MASS)

# LOOCV for LDA (built into MASS::lda!)
lda_cv <- lda(Species ~ ., data = iris, CV = TRUE)

# Honest classification accuracy
cv_accuracy <- mean(lda_cv$class == iris$Species)
cat("LDA LOOCV Accuracy:", round(cv_accuracy, 3))

# Confusion matrix from CV
table(Predicted = lda_cv$class, Actual = iris$Species)

# Compare with resubstitution (training accuracy — optimistic!)
lda_train <- lda(Species ~ ., data = iris)
train_pred <- predict(lda_train, iris)$class
train_accuracy <- mean(train_pred == iris$Species)
cat("\nTraining Accuracy:", round(train_accuracy, 3))
cat("\nCV Accuracy:     ", round(cv_accuracy, 3))
cat("\nDifference:      ", round(train_accuracy - cv_accuracy, 3))




# Compare LDA vs. KNN vs. SVM via 10-fold CV
library(caret)
set.seed(42)
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

# LDA
lda_cv_fit <- train(Species ~ ., data = iris, method = "lda",
                    trControl = ctrl)
# KNN
knn_cv_fit <- train(Species ~ ., data = iris, method = "knn",
                    trControl = ctrl, tuneGrid = data.frame(k = 1:15))
# SVM
svm_cv_fit <- train(Species ~ ., data = iris, method = "svmRadial",
                    trControl = ctrl)

# Compare results
results <- resamples(list(LDA = lda_cv_fit, KNN = knn_cv_fit, SVM = svm_cv_fit))
summary(results)
dotplot(results)

Principal components: new axes that maximize variance
Eigenvalues: amount of variance explained by each PC
Loadings: contribution of original variables to each PC
Scores: coordinates of observations in PC space

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
PCoA — Principal Coordinates Analysis
PCoA (also called classical multidimensional scaling) is similar to PCA but works on a dissimilarity matrix rather than raw data:

Can use any distance metric (Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, UniFrac, etc.)
Metric ordination: preserves actual distances
Scores can be used in downstream linear models


CodeWhen to Use



library(vegan)

# Calculate distance matrix
dist_matrix <- vegdist(my_data, method = "bray")

# Run PCoA
pcoa_result <- cmdscale(dist_matrix, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Plot
plot(pcoa_result$points, col = group_factor, pch = 19,
     xlab = "PCoA1", ylab = "PCoA2",
     main = "Principal Coordinates Analysis")




When your dissimilarity metric matters (e.g., ecological data with Bray-Curtis)
When you want metric ordination scores for downstream analysis
When data are not suited for PCA (e.g., count data, presence/absence)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
PCoA: Community Data Example

OutputCodePERMANOVA Notes














library(vegan)

# Calculate Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
dist_bc <- vegdist(community_data, method = "bray")

# Run PCoA
pcoa_res <- cmdscale(dist_bc, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Percent variance explained
var_exp <- round(100 * pcoa_res$eig[1:2] /
                 sum(pcoa_res$eig[pcoa_res$eig > 0]), 1)

# Plot with group labels
plot(pcoa_res$points, col = treatment, pch = 19,
     xlab = paste0("PCoA1 (", var_exp[1], "%)"),
     ylab = paste0("PCoA2 (", var_exp[2], "%)"),
     main = "PCoA (Bray-Curtis)")

# PERMANOVA: test if groups differ in multivariate space
adonis_result <- adonis2(dist_bc ~ treatment, permutations = 999)
print(adonis_result)

# Effect size: R² from PERMANOVA
cat("R² =", round(adonis_result$R2[1], 3))




PERMANOVA (adonis2()) tests whether group centroids differ in multivariate space
Works on any distance matrix (doesn’t require normality)
R² gives the proportion of variation explained by the grouping
Check betadisper() for homogeneity of dispersions (analogous to Levene’s test)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10

NMDS — Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling
NMDS is a form of nonparametric ordination:

Uses rank-order of dissimilarities rather than exact values
Relaxes distributional assumptions
Excellent for ecological, expression, and phenotypic data
Works well when relationships are non-linear

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10

NMDS Algorithm

Calculate dissimilarity matrix between samples
Place points in reduced dimensional space (usually 2D)
Iteratively adjust positions to minimize stress
Stress measures how well ordination distances match dissimilarities

Interpretation

0.05–0.10

> 0.20
Poor fit

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
NMDS: Hypothesis Testing with PERMANOVA

CodeInterpretation



library(vegan)

# Fit NMDS
nmds <- metaMDS(community_data, distance = "bray", k = 2, trymax = 100)

# PERMANOVA — test group differences on the distance matrix
dist_bc <- vegdist(community_data, method = "bray")
perm_result <- adonis2(dist_bc ~ treatment, permutations = 999)
print(perm_result)

# Check dispersion homogeneity (assumption of PERMANOVA)
disp <- betadisper(dist_bc, treatment)
permutest(disp, permutations = 999)

# envfit — fit environmental variables onto ordination
env_data <- data.frame(pH = rnorm(nrow(community_data), 7, 0.5),
                       temperature = rnorm(nrow(community_data), 37, 2))
ef <- envfit(nmds, env_data, permutations = 999)
print(ef)

# Plot NMDS with envfit vectors
plot(nmds, type = "n", main = "NMDS with Environmental Vectors")
points(nmds, col = treatment, pch = 19)
plot(ef, p.max = 0.05, col = "red", lwd = 2)




PERMANOVA (adonis2): Tests whether group centroids differ; report R² and p-value
betadisper: Checks if groups have similar spread (a PERMANOVA assumption)
envfit: Fits continuous environmental variables as vectors onto the ordination; arrow direction and length show correlation strength
Only plot envfit vectors that are significant (p < 0.05)

When to Use Each Dimensionality Reduction Method






Recommendations



PCA: Initial exploration, feature extraction, preprocessing, when you need interpretable axes
PCoA: When your distance metric matters (ecology, microbiome data)
NMDS: When rank-order relationships are more meaningful than exact distances
t-SNE: Publication-quality visualization of clusters in high-dimensional data
UMAP: Large datasets, when you need both global and local structure preserved

Decision Trees

Supervised learning using tree-like decision structure

Decision tree structure

Bioengineering decision tree example for injury risk

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
How Decision Trees Work

Start with entire dataset at root
Find best feature and split point (minimize impurity)
Create branches for each outcome
Repeat until stopping criteria met
Assign predictions to leaf nodes

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
Splitting Criteria

EquationsLaTeX


Gini Impurity (classification): \[Gini = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i^2\]
Entropy (classification): \[Entropy = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i \log_2(p_i)\]
MSE (regression trees): \[MSE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2\]


Gini = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i^2

Entropy = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i \log_2(p_i)

MSE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2

Decision Trees in R

CodePruning



library(rpart)

# Fit a classification tree
tree_model <- rpart(Species ~ ., data = iris, method = "class")

# Plot the tree

# Predict

table(Predicted = tree_pred, Actual = test_data$Species)




# View complexity parameter table
printcp(tree_model)

# Prune to optimal tree (minimize cross-validated error)

pruned_tree <- prune(tree_model, cp = optimal_cp)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
Decision Tree: Complete Pruning Workflow

OutputCode














library(rpart)

# Step 1: Grow a complex tree (low cp)
tree_full <- rpart(Species ~ ., data = iris, method = "class",
                   control = rpart.control(cp = 0.001))

# Step 2: Plot CV error by complexity parameter
plotcp(tree_full)

# Step 3: Find optimal cp (1-SE rule)
cp_table <- tree_full$cptable
optimal_cp <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"]), "CP"]

# Step 4: Prune
pruned_tree <- prune(tree_full, cp = optimal_cp)

# Step 5: Better visualization with rpart.plot
# install.packages("rpart.plot")
library(rpart.plot)
rpart.plot(pruned_tree, type = 4, extra = 104,
           box.palette = "BuGn",
           main = "Pruned Classification Tree")

Build many trees on bootstrap samples of the data
Randomly select a subset of features at each split

Advantages: Reduces overfitting, more stable predictions, handles high-dimensional data, provides variable importance measures

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
Brief Introduction to Neural Networks
Neural networks extend the ideas of linear regression and classification into highly flexible models:

Layers of interconnected nodes (neurons) transform inputs
Each connection has a learned weight
Non-linear activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid) allow complex decision boundaries
Trained by backpropagation — iteratively adjusting weights to minimize a loss function







Note


Neural networks are powerful but require large datasets, careful tuning, and are often “black boxes” that are difficult to interpret. For most bioengineering applications with moderate sample sizes, methods like random forests, SVM, or regularized regression are more appropriate starting points.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
Simple Neural Network in R

CodeKey Points



library(nnet)

# Scale predictors for neural network
iris_scaled <- iris
iris_scaled[, 1:4] <- scale(iris[, 1:4])

# Train/test split
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(iris_scaled), 0.7 * nrow(iris_scaled))
train <- iris_scaled[train_idx, ]
test  <- iris_scaled[-train_idx, ]

# Fit single hidden layer neural network
nn_model <- nnet(Species ~ ., data = train,
                 size = 5,       # 5 hidden neurons
                 decay = 0.01,   # weight decay (regularization)
                 maxit = 500,
                 trace = FALSE)

# Predictions and accuracy
nn_pred <- predict(nn_model, test, type = "class")
accuracy <- mean(nn_pred == test$Species)
cat("Neural Network Accuracy:", round(accuracy, 3))
table(Predicted = nn_pred, Actual = test$Species)

# Compare with random forest
library(randomForest)
rf_model <- randomForest(Species ~ ., data = train)
rf_pred <- predict(rf_model, test)
cat("\nRandom Forest Accuracy:", round(mean(rf_pred == test$Species), 3))




nnet implements a single hidden layer — sufficient for many problems
size: number of hidden neurons (start small, increase if underfitting)
decay: L2 regularization to prevent overfitting
Always scale inputs before training a neural network
For deep learning, explore keras and tensorflow packages
This is a brief introduction — take a dedicated ML course for depth

Which Method Should I Use?
Start by asking these questions:

What is your goal? Inference (understanding) vs. Prediction
What type is your response variable? Continuous, binary, count, time-to-event, multivariate
How many predictors? Few vs. many; continuous vs. categorical vs. mixed
Sample size? Small (n < 30), moderate (30–200), large (200+)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 10
text:
Method Selection: Inference









Response

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 4
text:
Calculating Cramér’s V in R

OutputCode




Cramér's V: 0.49





# Chi-square test of independence
test <- chisq.test(tbl)

# Extract test statistic
chisq_val <- test$statistic

# Total number of observations
n <- sum(tbl)

# Minimum of (rows, columns) for Cramér's V formula
k <- min(nrow(tbl), ncol(tbl))

# Cramér's V calculation
cramers_v <- sqrt(chisq_val / (n * (k - 1)))

cat("Cramér's V:", round(cramers_v, 3))

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 4
text:
Odds Ratios
Compares odds of an event between two groups:

OR = 1: No association
OR > 1: Group 1 has higher odds
OR < 1: Group 1 has lower odds

Example:

Odds (Americans prefer Coffee) = \(\frac{8}{2} = 4\)
Odds (English prefer Coffee) = \(\frac{1}{9} ≈ 0.111\)
Odds Ratio = \(\frac{4}{0.111} ≈ 36\)







Note


The chi-square test tells us whether there is a difference, but the odds ratio tells us the effect size - how much more likely one outcome is compared to another.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 4
text:
Covariance and Correlation

Simple but useful measures of association between two or more continuous variables
Covariance is the shared variance and scales with the variance of the variables
Correlcation is a standardized covariance to put the values on a common scale
Both are useful but suboptimal compared to linear models.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 4
text:
Covariance and Correlation
Covariance Measures how two variables vary together:

EquationLaTeX


\[Cov(X,Y) = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n-1}\]


Cov(X,Y) = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n-1}



Correlation does the same thing but is a standardized covariance (ranges from -1 to 1):

EquationLaTeX


\[r = \frac{Cov(X,Y)}{s_x \cdot s_y}\]


r = \frac{Cov(X,Y)}{s_x \cdot s_y}




Positive: variables increase together
Negative: one increases as other decreases
Zero: no linear relationship

par(mfrow = c(1, 4))

# Function to generate correlated data
make_corr_data <- function(r, n = 100) {
  x <- rnorm(n)
  y <- r * x + sqrt(1 - r^2) * rnorm(n)
  data.frame(x = x, y = y)
}

correlations <- c(-0.9, -0.3, 0.3, 0.9)
for(r in correlations) {
  d <- make_corr_data(r)
  plot(d$x, d$y, pch = 19, col = rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.5),
       main = paste("r =", r), xlab = "X", ylab = "Y")

}

Last week we introduced Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA), which combines:

Categorical predictor (factor) — like species or treatment

This week we continue with the biological motivations, interpretation, and assumptions.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text: ANCOVA: Adjusted Means

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
DRAFT: ANCOVA Adjusted Means
The ANCOVA model:
\[y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta(x_{ij} - \bar{x}) + \varepsilon_{ij}\]
Adjusted means are computed at the overall mean of the covariate:
\[\bar{y}_{i(adj)} = \bar{y}_i - \hat{\beta}(\bar{x}_i - \bar{x})\]

The key insight: by adjusting for the covariate, we can compare groups at the same value of the continuous predictor, removing confounding variation.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text: ANCOVA: Multiple Covariates

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
DRAFT: ANCOVA with Multiple Covariates
Linear model:
\[y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_1(x_{1ij} - \bar{x}_1) + \beta_2(x_{2ij} - \bar{x}_2) + \varepsilon_{ij}\]
Adjusted mean:
\[\bar{y}_{i(adj)} = \bar{y}_i - \hat{\beta}_1(\bar{x}_{1i} - \bar{x}_1) - \hat{\beta}_2(\bar{x}_{2i} - \bar{x}_2)\]

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text: ANCOVA: Null Hypotheses

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
DRAFT: ANCOVA Null Hypotheses
For the categorical factor (e.g., species):
\[H_0: \mu_{1(adj)} = \mu_{2(adj)} = \ldots = \mu_{p(adj)}\]
All adjusted group means are equal (after accounting for the covariate).
For the covariate (e.g., body mass):
\[H_0: \beta = 0\]
The covariate has no linear relationship with the response.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text: ANCOVA: F-Ratio Table and Collinearity

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:

Source
df
MS
F-ratio




Factor A
\(p - 1\)
\(MS_A\)
\(MS_A / MS_{Residual}\)


Covariate
1
\(MS_{Covariate}\)
\(MS_{Cov} / MS_{Residual}\)


Residual
\(N - p - 1\)
\(MS_{Residual}\)










Collinearity in ANCOVA


If the covariate and the factor are correlated (e.g., body mass differs between species), the order in which terms enter the model matters. Use Type II or Type III sums of squares from the car package to handle this properly.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text: ANCOVA: Heterogeneous Slopes

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
DRAFT: Heterogeneous Slopes

When slopes differ between groups, the interaction between the covariate and the factor is significant — this is a violation of the parallel slopes assumption.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Parallel Slopes (Additive) Model
When there is no interaction, each group has the same slope but different intercepts:

EquationLaTeX


\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{continuous} + \beta_2 x_{categorical} + \epsilon_i\]


y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{continuous} + \beta_2 x_{categorical} + \epsilon_i




# Parallel slopes model (additive)
lm(response ~ continuous_var + factor_var, data = mydata)


The + means “additive” — the effect of the covariate is the same in every group
This produces parallel regression lines

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Interaction Model
When the relationship differs between groups, add an interaction term:

EquationLaTeX


\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 (x_1 \times x_2) + \epsilon_i\]


y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 (x_1 \times x_2) + \epsilon_i




# Model with interaction (different slopes)
lm(response ~ continuous_var * factor_var, data = mydata)

# Equivalent to:
lm(response ~ continuous_var + factor_var + continuous_var:factor_var,
   data = mydata)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Interpreting ANCOVA Output

CodeInterpretation



# Example with crickets data
lm(rate ~ temp + species, data = crickets)

# Output interpretation:
# (Intercept)      - baseline intercept for reference level
# temp             - slope (same for all groups)
# speciesO.niveus  - difference in intercept from reference




The categorical variable coefficient represents the offset from the reference group
This is the same dummy variable encoding that lm() uses for ANOVA
The only difference from pure ANOVA is the inclusion of a continuous predictor

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
section: Parallel vs. Interaction: When to Use
text:
Parallel vs. Interaction: When to Use








Model
Use When
R Formula




Parallel Slopes
Effect of covariate is same across groups
y ~ x + group


Interaction
Effect of covariate differs by group
y ~ x * group









Tip


Always start with the interaction model. Test whether the interaction term is significant. If not, drop it and use the simpler parallel slopes model (parsimony principle).

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
section: ANCOVA: Type II/III Sums of Squares
text:
ANCOVA: Type II/III Sums of Squares

CodeWhen to Use



library(car)

# Type II SS — tests each term after adjusting for all others
# (appropriate when no significant interaction)
Anova(lm(y ~ covariate + factor, data = mydata), type = "II")

# Type III SS — tests each term after adjusting for all others
# including interaction (appropriate when interaction is present)
Anova(lm(y ~ covariate * factor, data = mydata), type = "III")











SS Type
Use When
Notes




Type I
Balanced designs, order matters
Default in anova()


Type II
Unbalanced, no interaction
Default in car::Anova()


Type III
Unbalanced, interaction present
Requires contr.sum coding

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Dangers of Extrapolation
All regression models (including ANCOVA) are only valid within the range of the observed data:

Polynomial models are especially dangerous to extrapolate — they can produce wildly unrealistic predictions outside the data range
Even linear ANCOVA predictions become unreliable far from the observed covariate values
Always report the range of your covariates alongside your model







Rule of Thumb


Never predict beyond the range of your observed data unless you have strong theoretical justification for the extrapolation.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Why Multiple Regression?
Multiple linear regression extends simple regression to include two or more predictor variables. The goals are:

Develop a better predictive model than possible from models based on single independent variables
Investigate the relative individual effects of each predictor variable above and beyond the effects of the other variables
The individual effects of each predictor on the response can be depicted by partial regression lines
The slope of any partial regression line represents the rate of change of that predictor on the response, holding all other predictors constant at their means

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Additive and Multiplicative Models
Additive model — each predictor contributes independently:

EquationLaTeX


\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \ldots + \beta_j x_{ij} + \epsilon_i\]


y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \ldots + \beta_j x_{ij} + \epsilon_i



Multiplicative model — includes an interaction between two predictors:

EquationLaTeX


\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \beta_3 x_{i1} x_{i2} + \epsilon_i\]


y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \beta_3 x_{i1} x_{i2} + \epsilon_i

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Multiple Regression Assumptions
Multiple regression carries all the assumptions of simple regression plus an additional one:

Linearity — the relationship between predictors and response is linear
Normality — residuals are normally distributed
Homogeneity of variance — constant variance of residuals
Independence — observations are independent
No multicollinearity — a predictor variable must not be strongly correlated with the combination of other predictor variables







Multicollinearity


When predictors are highly correlated, coefficient estimates become unstable, standard errors inflate, and interpretation becomes unreliable. Always check for collinearity before interpreting a multiple regression model.

vif(model)

# Tolerance = 1/VIF (values < 0.1 indicate severe collinearity)
1 / vif(model)

Bioengineering Example: Scaffold Properties and Tissue Growth

CodeQuestions



# Simulated bioengineering data: predicting tissue growth
# from scaffold porosity, stiffness, and cell seeding density
set.seed(42)
n <- 60

scaffold_data <- data.frame(
  porosity     = runif(n, 40, 90),         # percent porosity
  stiffness    = runif(n, 5, 50),          # kPa
  seeding_dens = runif(n, 1e4, 1e6)        # cells/mL
)
scaffold_data$tissue_growth <- with(scaffold_data,
  0.8 * porosity + 0.3 * stiffness - 0.00001 * seeding_dens +
  0.005 * porosity * stiffness + rnorm(n, 0, 8)
)

# Fit multiple regression
scaffold_lm <- lm(tissue_growth ~ porosity + stiffness + seeding_dens,
                   data = scaffold_data)
summary(scaffold_lm)

Model Selection Criteria








Criterion
Description
Selection Rule




MSresiduals
Mean unexplained variation
Lowest value = best fit


Adjusted R²
Proportion of variance explained, penalized for # terms
Larger = better fit


Mallow’s Cp
Comparison to full model
Lowest value, or closest to p


AIC
Likelihood penalized by number of parameters
Smaller = more parsimonious


BIC
Like AIC but heavier penalty for complexity
Smaller = more parsimonious









Tip


As a rule of thumb, if the difference between two AIC values (ΔAIC) is greater than 2, the lower AIC represents a meaningfully better model.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text: Mallow’s Cp and All-Subsets Regression

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
DRAFT: Mallow’s Cp Formula

EquationLaTeX


\[C_p = \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{\hat{\sigma}^2} - n + 2p\]
where:







Symbol
Meaning




\(SS_{\text{error}}\)
Error sum of squares for the model with \(p\) predictors (incl. intercept)


\(\hat{\sigma}^2\)
Error mean square of full model (e.g., all predictors)


\(n\)
Sample size


\(p\)
Number of predictors (including intercept)




\(C_p\) estimates mean square prediction error (related to AIC)
\(2p\): a penalty for including too many predictors — a feature shared with all other model selection criteria



C_p = \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{\hat{\sigma}^2} - n + 2p




CodeKey Points



library(leaps)

# All subsets regression
all_subsets <- regsubsets(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3 + g4, data = RNAseq_Data)
summary(all_subsets)

# Plot Cp, BIC, adjusted R²
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(all_subsets, scale = "Cp")
plot(all_subsets, scale = "bic")
plot(all_subsets, scale = "adjr2")




For prediction: All models with Cp < p predict about equally well
For explanation: If numerous models fit equally well, it is difficult to deduce which predictor “explains” the response
General caveat: “Regression is not causation” — an experiment is needed for causal explanation

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Nested vs. Non-Nested Models

Nested (reduced vs. full): One model is a special case of the other — can compare with F-test or likelihood ratio test
Non-nested: Models contain different sets of variables — compare with AIC or BIC


CodeInterpretation



# Compare nested models with F-test
model_reduced <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2)
model_full    <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3)
anova(model_reduced, model_full)

# Compare non-nested models with AIC
AIC(model_a, model_b, model_c)
BIC(model_a, model_b, model_c)




F-test p < 0.05 → the fuller model is significantly better
Lower AIC/BIC → more parsimonious model
BIC penalizes complexity more heavily than AIC

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Stepwise Model Selection in R

CodeKey Points



# Start with a full model
full_model <- lm(tissue_growth ~ porosity * stiffness * seeding_dens,
                 data = scaffold_data)

# Forward stepwise selection (start from intercept-only)
null_model <- lm(tissue_growth ~ 1, data = scaffold_data)
forward_model <- step(null_model,
                      scope = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_model),
                      direction = "forward", trace = 1)

# Backward elimination (start from full model)
backward_model <- step(full_model, direction = "backward", trace = 1)

# Both directions
both_model <- step(null_model,
                   scope = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_model),
                   direction = "both", trace = 1)

# Compare final models
AIC(forward_model, backward_model, both_model)
BIC(forward_model, backward_model, both_model)




step() uses AIC by default; add k = log(n) for BIC-based selection
Forward selection can miss important combinations
Backward elimination can fail when p > n
“Both” direction is generally most robust
Stepwise methods can overfit — always validate with cross-validation

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
What is Power?
Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (i.e., detecting a real effect when one exists).

EquationLaTeX


\[\text{Power} \propto \frac{(\text{Effect Size})(\alpha)(\sqrt{n})}{\sigma}\]


\text{Power} \propto \frac{(\text{Effect Size})(\alpha)(\sqrt{n})}{\sigma}




Helps interpret failure to reject the null — was the test underpowered?
Target: typically 80% power (β = 0.20)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7

Power Overview

Statistical power and Type II error

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
section: DRAFT: Statistical Power and Type II Error
text:
DRAFT: Statistical Power and Type II Error









Reject \(H_0\)
Retain \(H_0\)




Effect exists
Correct decision — Effect detected (Power = \(1-\beta\))
Type II error — Effect not detected (\(\beta\))


No effect
Type I error — Effect detected; none exists (\(\alpha\))
Correct decision — No effect detected









Note



Power = probability of correctly rejecting \(H_0\) when the effect is real
We want Power \(\geq 0.80\) (i.e., \(\beta \leq 0.20\))
Increasing sample size, effect size, or \(\alpha\) increases power

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Bootstrap Power Analysis
When parametric assumptions may not hold, use simulation-based power analysis:

CodeKey Points



# Step 1: Simulate true populations
senior <- rpois(5000, lambda = 10)
fresh  <- rpois(5000, lambda = 12)

# Step 2: Draw samples and test
sample_s <- sample(senior, size = 10, replace = FALSE)
sample_f <- sample(fresh, size = 10, replace = FALSE)
t.test(sample_f, sample_s)

# Step 3: Replicate many times
samps_s <- replicate(n = 100, sample(senior, size = 10))
samps_f <- replicate(n = 100, sample(fresh, size = 10))

# Calculate power
tests <- data.frame(result = numeric(100))
for (i in 1:100) {
  tests$result[i] <- t.test(samps_s[, i], samps_f[, i])$p.value
}
power <- sum(tests$result < 0.05) / 100
cat("Estimated power:", power)




This approach works for any distribution (Poisson, skewed, etc.)
Increase the number of replicates (e.g., 1000+) for stable estimates
Can modify sample sizes, effect sizes, or distributions to explore scenarios

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Power Analysis for ANOVA

CodeCohen’s f



library(pwr)

# Parameters for one-way ANOVA
effect_size_anova <- 0.25  # Cohen's f (medium)
alpha_anova <- 0.05
power_anova <- 0.8

# Calculate required sample size per group
sample_size_anova <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = 3,                    # Number of groups
  f = effect_size_anova,
  sig.level = alpha_anova,
  power = power_anova
)$n

cat("Sample Size per group for ANOVA:", ceiling(sample_size_anova))



Cohen’s f measures effect size in ANOVA:



f
Interpretation




0.10
Small effect


0.25
Medium effect


0.40
Large effect



Cohen’s f = √(variance between groups / variance within groups)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Power Example: Bone Scaffold Experiment
A bioengineering lab needs to determine how many bone scaffolds to test to detect a 15% difference in compressive strength between two scaffold designs.

CodeKey Takeaway



# Known from pilot data:
# Mean compressive strength: 50 MPa
# Standard deviation: 8 MPa
# Desired detectable difference: 15% = 7.5 MPa

effect_size_d <- 7.5 / 8  # Cohen's d = 0.94

scaffold_power <- pwr.t.test(
  d = effect_size_d,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80,
  type = "two.sample"
)

cat("Required scaffolds per group:", ceiling(scaffold_power$n))
cat("\nEffect size (Cohen's d):", round(effect_size_d, 2))




With a large effect size (d ≈ 0.94), we need relatively few samples
If the expected difference were only 5% (3.75 MPa, d ≈ 0.47), sample size would roughly quadruple
Always conduct a power analysis before running your experiment

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Power for Factorial ANOVA

CodeTip



library(pwr)

# Power for a 2×3 factorial design
# (e.g., 2 scaffold materials × 3 growth factor concentrations)
pwr.anova.test(
  k = 6,           # Total number of cells (2 × 3)
  f = 0.30,        # Medium-large effect
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)

# For interaction effects specifically:
# Interactions are typically harder to detect
# Use a smaller f value or plan for more samples
pwr.anova.test(
  k = 6,
  f = 0.20,        # Small-medium for interaction
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)



Interactions typically have smaller effect sizes than main effects. Budget extra samples if detecting interactions is important to your study.

One level of nesting:

DRAFT: Hypotheses in Nested Designs

Fixed Effects (Main Factor)Random EffectsLaTeX


\[H_0(A): \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \ldots = \mu_i = \mu \quad \text{(in terms of pop. means)}\]
\[H_0(A): \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \ldots = \alpha_i = 0 \quad \text{(in terms of effects on the grand mean)}\]


\[H_0(A): \sigma^2_\alpha = 0\]
“No added variance due to all possible levels of A”
\[H_0(B): \sigma^2_\beta = 0\]
“No added variance due to all possible levels of B within all possible levels of A”

H_0(A): \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \ldots = \alpha_i = 0

% Random effects
H_0(A): \sigma^2_\alpha = 0

Factorial vs. Nested Designs
Factorial designs:

All pairwise combinations of factor levels are present
Can assess interactions between factors
Example: Drug dose × Exercise regimen

Nested designs:

Hierarchical structure — levels of one factor occur within levels of another
No interaction terms (levels are unique to each group)
Often contain random effects
Example: Cells within wells within plates

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
DRAFT: Two-Factor Factorial Model

EquationLaTeX


\[\huge y_{ijk} = \mu + \underbrace{\alpha_i + \beta_j}_{\text{Main Effects}} + \underbrace{(\alpha\beta)_{ij}}_{\text{Two-way interaction}} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]
where:

\(\mu\) = grand mean
\(\alpha_i\) = effect of level \(i\) of factor A
\(\beta_j\) = effect of level \(j\) of factor B
\((\alpha\beta)_{ij}\) = interaction effect of A level \(i\) and B level \(j\)
\(\varepsilon_{ijk}\) = random error for replicate \(k\)



y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}

Term
Meaning




\(\alpha_i, \beta_j, \gamma_k\)
Main effects of factors A, B, C

DRAFT: Interpreting Significant Terms

ModelWhen All Terms Are SignificantLaTeX


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

Factor 1 is temperature
Factor 2 is fertilizer



If all terms in the model are significant — now what?

Start with the interaction — if \((\alpha\beta)_{ij}\) is significant, the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other
Main effects are hard to interpret alone when interaction is present
Examine simple effects — the effect of one factor at each level of the other
Use interaction plots to visualize patterns
Perform post-hoc comparisons within each level of the other factor

Factorial ANOVA in R

CodeInterpretation



rna_data <- read.table("data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv", header = TRUE, sep = "\t")

gene       <- rna_data$Gene100
microbiota <- rna_data$Microbiota
genotype   <- rna_data$Genotype

# Multiplicative model (with interaction)
model_interaction <- aov(gene ~ microbiota * genotype)

# Additive model (no interaction)
model_additive <- aov(gene ~ microbiota + genotype)

summary(model_interaction)
summary(model_additive)




If the interaction term is significant, the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other
If the interaction is not significant, interpret the main effects directly
Always check the interaction first before interpreting main effects

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Fixed vs. Random Effects
Fixed effects:

Groups are predetermined, of direct interest, repeatable
Examples: medical treatments, predetermined doses, habitat types
We want to estimate specific group means

Random effects:

Groups randomly sampled from a larger population
Examples: families, subjects measured repeatedly, blocks, batches
Variance among groups is of interest, not specific group means

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
When to Use Random Effects

Nested sampling designs (individuals within populations)
Subplots within plots
Replicates grouped spatially or temporally (blocks, batches)
Related individuals (families, litters)
Repeated measures on the same subjects

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7

EquationLaTeX


\[H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0\] \[H_A: \sigma^2_\alpha \neq 0\]


H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0
H_A: \sigma^2_\alpha \neq 0



We are testing whether the variance component for the random effect is zero — i.e., whether there is meaningful variation among the randomly sampled groups.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Random Effects in R

CodeKey Points



library(nlme)

# Random effect model
micro_model_random_effect <- lme(
  fixed  = Gene202 ~ 1,
  random = ~1 | Geno.Micro,
  data   = stickle_micro
)

summary(micro_model_random_effect)




In R, lm() assumes all effects are fixed
For random effects, use lme() from the nlme package or lmer() from lme4
The ~1 | group syntax specifies a random intercept for each level of group

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Random Effects: Bioengineering Example
Measuring cell viability across multiple wells within multiple plates within multiple experiments:

CodeInterpreting Variance Components



# Simulated hierarchical data: cells → wells → plates → experiments
set.seed(42)
n_exp <- 3; n_plate <- 4; n_well <- 6
experiment <- rep(1:n_exp, each = n_plate * n_well)
plate      <- rep(rep(1:n_plate, each = n_well), n_exp)
well       <- rep(1:n_well, n_exp * n_plate)

# Generate data with variance at each level
exp_effect   <- rnorm(n_exp, 0, 5)[experiment]
plate_effect <- rnorm(n_exp * n_plate, 0, 3)[interaction(experiment, plate)]
viability    <- 75 + exp_effect + plate_effect + rnorm(n_exp * n_plate * n_well, 0, 2)

cell_data <- data.frame(
  viability, experiment = factor(experiment),
  plate = factor(plate), well = factor(well)
)

# Fit nested random effects model
library(nlme)
nested_model <- lme(viability ~ 1,
                    random = ~1 | experiment/plate,
                    data = cell_data)
summary(nested_model)

# Extract variance components
VarCorr(nested_model)



The output from VarCorr() shows:

Experiment variance: variation between experimental runs
Plate-within-experiment variance: variation between plates within a run
Residual variance: well-to-well variation within plates
ICC (Intraclass Correlation) = group variance / total variance

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Nested Design

Factors are hierarchical within one another
Sources of variance are hierarchical
No interaction terms (in completely nested designs)

Example: Students within classrooms within schools

CodeInterpretation



# Nested ANOVA using aov
model_nested <- aov(y ~ A + B %in% A, data = mydata)

# Using lme for random nested effects
model_nested_random <- lme(y ~ A, random = ~1 | A/B, data = mydata)

summary(model_nested_random)




The %in% notation means “B is nested within A”
The ~1 | A/B random effects specification means “random intercepts for B nested within A”
Nested designs arise when the levels of one factor are unique to each level of another (e.g., specific cell lines unique to each lab)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
What are Repeated Measures?
Measurements taken on the same subjects at multiple:

Time points (longitudinal studies)
Conditions (within-subjects design)
Locations (spatial sampling)

Advantages: Controls for individual differences, requires fewer subjects, more statistical power
Challenge: Observations are not independent — standard ANOVA assumes independence

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 7
text:
Repeated Measures ANOVA
Sphericity Assumption:

Variances of differences between all pairs of conditions must be equal
Often violated in practice

Mauchly’s Test: Tests the sphericity assumption

p < 0.05 → sphericity is violated → apply correction (Greenhouse-Geisser or Huynh-Feldt)

Precision: closeness of repeated estimates to each other
Replication quantifies variation
Randomization avoids bias

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Stochastic Processes in Statistics

We often want to know truths about the world, but can only estimate them
Uncertainty in those estimates is a given
Statistics is largely about quantifying and managing uncertainty
Random variables are products of stochastic processes
Expectations are based on theoretical probability distributions

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Two Interpretations of Probability
Frequency interpretation:
“Probabilities are mathematically convenient approximations to long run relative frequencies.”
Subjective (Bayesian) interpretation:
“A probability statement expresses the opinion of some individual regarding how certain an event is to occur.”

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Random Variables and Probability

Probability is the expression of belief in some future outcome
A random variable can take on different values with different probabilities
The sample space is the universe of all possible values
Sample space represented by:

Probability mass distribution (discrete)
Probability density function (continuous)








Important


Probabilities of a sample space always sum to 1.0

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Probability Rules
‘And’ rule (multiplication):

EquationLaTeX


\[Pr(X \text{ and } Y) = Pr(X) \times Pr(Y)\]


Pr(X \text{ and } Y) = Pr(X) \times Pr(Y)



‘Or’ rule (addition):

EquationLaTeX


\[Pr(X \text{ or } Y) = Pr(X) + Pr(Y)\]


Pr(X \text{ or } Y) = Pr(X) + Pr(Y)









Note


The ‘and’ rule assumes independent events. For non-independent events, we need conditional probabilities.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Joint and Conditional Probability
Joint probability (independent events):

EquationLaTeX


\[Pr(X,Y) = Pr(X) \times Pr(Y)\]


Pr(X,Y) = Pr(X) \times Pr(Y)



Conditional probability (independent):
\[Pr(Y|X) = Pr(Y) \text{ and } Pr(X|Y) = Pr(X)\]
Conditional probability (non-independent):
\[Pr(Y|X) \neq Pr(Y) \text{ and } Pr(X|Y) \neq Pr(X)\]

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Likelihood vs. Probability

Probability: proportion of times an event would occur over many trials
Likelihood: conditional probability of a parameter value given data


EquationLaTeX


\[L[\text{parameter}|\text{data}] = Pr[\text{data}|\text{parameter}]\]


L[\text{parameter}|\text{data}] = Pr[\text{data}|\text{parameter}]




Maximum likelihood: highest value of the likelihood function
Bayesian estimate: uses prior distribution to update posterior distribution

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Moments of Distributions
1st moment (mean/expectation):

EquationLaTeX


\[E[X] = \sum_{\text{all x}}xP(X=x) = \mu\]


E[X] = \sum_{\text{all x}}xP(X=x) = \mu



2nd moment (variance):

EquationLaTeX


\[Var(X) = E[(X-\mu)^2] = \sigma^2\]


Var(X) = E[(X-\mu)^2] = \sigma^2



Standard deviation: \[SD = \sqrt{\sigma^2} = \sigma\]
Higher moments include skewness (3rd) and kurtosis (4th).

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Bernoulli Distribution
Describes the expected outcome of a single event with probability \(p\).
Example: Flipping a fair coin once
\[Pr(X=\text{Head}) = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5 = p\]
\[Pr(X=\text{Tails}) = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5 = 1 - p = q\]
Probabilities always sum to 1: \(p + q = 1\)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
section: In-Class Demo: Law of Large Numbers with Coin Flips
text:
In-Class Demo: Law of Large Numbers with Coin Flips
Watch how the proportion of heads converges to 0.5 as we flip more coins:

OutputCode














set.seed(344)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

# Different sample sizes
for(n in c(1, 8, 16, 32, 400, 1000)) {
  flips <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.5)  # 0 = heads, 1 = tails
  prop_heads <- sum(flips == 0) / length(flips)
  prop_tails <- 1 - prop_heads

  barplot(height = c(prop_heads, prop_tails),
          names.arg = c("heads", "tails"),
          col = c("steelblue", "coral"),
          ylim = c(0, 1),
          main = paste("n =", n, "flips"),
          ylab = "Proportion")
  abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "gray")
}










Tip


As sample size increases, observed proportions converge to true probability (0.5).

Poisson Distribution
For discrete counts (e.g., snails per plot, neuron firings per second).

EquationLaTeX


\[Pr(Y=r) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^r}{r!}\]


Pr(Y=r) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^r}{r!}









Note


The Poisson is a single-parameter distribution: \(\mu = \sigma^2 = \lambda\)
Variables with variance > mean are called “overdispersed” (common in RNA-seq data).

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Geometric Distribution
Probability of observing \(k\) trials before the first success:
\[P(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p\]

Mean = \(\frac{1}{p}\)
Variance = \(\frac{(1-p)}{p^2}\)

Example: If extinction probability is 0.1 per year, expected time to extinction?

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Negative Binomial Distribution
Probability of the \(r^{th}\) success on the \(k^{th}\) trial:
\[P(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^{r}(1-p)^{k-r}\]

Mean = \(\frac{r}{p}\)
Variance = \(\frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}\)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Continuous Probability Distributions
\[P(a\leq X \leq b) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx\]
The indefinite integral sums to one:
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) dx = 1\]
Expectation: \[E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x) dx\]

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2

All outcomes equally probable.
\[E[X] = \frac{(a+b)}{2}\]

Exponential Distribution

EquationLaTeX


\[f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\]


f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}




\(E[X] = \frac{1}{\lambda}\)
\(Var(X) = \frac{1}{\lambda^2}\)

Example: If λ equals the instantaneous death rate, the lifespan follows an exponential distribution.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Gamma Distribution
Waiting time until the \(r^{th}\) event at rate \(\lambda\):
\[f(x) = \frac{\lambda^r x^{r-1} e^{-\lambda x}}{(r-1)!}\]

Mean = \(\frac{r}{\lambda}\)
Variance = \(\frac{r}{\lambda^2}\)

Example: Time until 1000 DNA strands synthesized at rate 1/ms.

Normal (Gaussian) Distribution

EquationLaTeX


\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \, \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]


f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \, \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}



Notation: \(v \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
CLT in Quantitative Genetics
Why are complex traits normally distributed?
Simulate a trait controlled by 5 genes, each with additive effects:

OutputCode














set.seed(245)
n_individuals <- 100

# Each locus contributes -1, 0, or +1 to phenotype (diploid genotypes)
contributions <- matrix(0, nrow = n_individuals, ncol = 5)
for(locus in 1:5) {
  genotype <- rbinom(n_individuals, size = 2, prob = 0.5)  # 0, 1, or 2 copies
  contributions[, locus] <- ifelse(genotype == 2, 1,
                                    ifelse(genotype == 1, 0, -1))
}

# Sum across loci to get phenotype
phenotype <- rowSums(contributions)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(phenotype, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
     main = "5-Locus Trait Distribution",
     xlab = "Phenotype Value", breaks = seq(-6, 6, 1))

# Add environmental noise to make continuous
phenotype_continuous <- phenotype + rnorm(n_individuals, 0, 0.5)
hist(phenotype_continuous, col = "coral", border = "white",
     main = "With Environmental Variation",
     xlab = "Phenotype Value", breaks = 20)










Note


This is why quantitative traits (height, weight, blood pressure) are approximately normal!

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Week 2
text:
Visualizing What “95% Confidence” Means

OutputCode










Figure 6: 95% of CIs from repeated sampling contain the true mean (μ = 10)








true_mean <- 10
n_samples <- 50

# Take 50 samples and calculate CIs
results <- t(replicate(n_samples, {
  samp <- rnorm(20, mean = true_mean, sd = 2)
  ci <- t.test(samp)$conf.int
  c(mean = mean(samp), lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])
}))

# Plot CIs - color red if they miss the true mean
contains_true <- results[, "lower"] <= true_mean & results[, "upper"] >= true_mean
colors <- ifelse(contains_true, "steelblue", "red")

plot(NULL, xlim = c(8, 12), ylim = c(0, n_samples + 1),
     xlab = "Value", ylab = "Sample Number", main = "50 Confidence Intervals")
abline(v = true_mean, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
for(i in 1:n_samples) {
  segments(results[i, "lower"], i, results[i, "upper"], i, col = colors[i], lwd = 2)
  points(results[i, "mean"], i, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = colors[i])
}
legend("topright", c(paste(sum(contains_true), "contain μ"),
       paste(sum(!contains_true), "miss μ")), col = c("steelblue", "red"), lwd = 2)

The key insight: by adjusting for the covariate, we can compare groups at the same value of the continuous predictor, removing confounding variation.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
ANCOVA: F-Ratio Table and Collinearity







Collinearity in ANCOVA


If the covariate and the factor are correlated (e.g., body mass differs between species), the order in which terms enter the model matters. Use Type II or Type III sums of squares from the car package to handle this properly.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
ANCOVA: Heterogeneous Slopes

When slopes differ between groups, the interaction between the covariate and the factor is significant — this is a violation of the parallel slopes assumption.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Parallel Slopes (Additive) Model
When there is no interaction, each group has the same slope but different intercepts:

EquationLaTeX


\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{continuous} + \beta_2 x_{categorical} + \epsilon_i\]


y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{continuous} + \beta_2 x_{categorical} + \epsilon_i




# Parallel slopes model (additive)
lm(response ~ continuous_var + factor_var, data = mydata)


The + means “additive” — the effect of the covariate is the same in every group
This produces parallel regression lines

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Interaction Model
When the relationship differs between groups, add an interaction term:

EquationLaTeX


\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 (x_1 \times x_2) + \epsilon_i\]


y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 (x_1 \times x_2) + \epsilon_i




# Model with interaction (different slopes)
lm(response ~ continuous_var * factor_var, data = mydata)

# Equivalent to:
lm(response ~ continuous_var + factor_var + continuous_var:factor_var,
   data = mydata)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Interpreting ANCOVA Output

CodeInterpretation



# Example with crickets data
lm(rate ~ temp + species, data = crickets)

# Output interpretation:
# (Intercept)      - baseline intercept for reference level
# temp             - slope (same for all groups)
# speciesO.niveus  - difference in intercept from reference




The categorical variable coefficient represents the offset from the reference group
This is the same dummy variable encoding that lm() uses for ANOVA
The only difference from pure ANOVA is the inclusion of a continuous predictor

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
section: Parallel vs. Interaction: When to Use
text:
Parallel vs. Interaction: When to Use








Model
Use When
R Formula




Parallel Slopes
Effect of covariate is same across groups
y ~ x + group


Interaction
Effect of covariate differs by group
y ~ x * group









Tip


Always start with the interaction model. Test whether the interaction term is significant. If not, drop it and use the simpler parallel slopes model (parsimony principle).

# Type III SS — tests each term after adjusting for all others
# including interaction (appropriate when interaction is present)

Use When

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Dangers of Extrapolation
All regression models (including ANCOVA) are only valid within the range of the observed data:

Polynomial models are especially dangerous to extrapolate — they can produce wildly unrealistic predictions outside the data range
Even linear ANCOVA predictions become unreliable far from the observed covariate values
Always report the range of your covariates alongside your model







Rule of Thumb


Never predict beyond the range of your observed data unless you have strong theoretical justification for the extrapolation.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Why Multiple Regression?
Multiple linear regression extends simple regression to include two or more predictor variables. The goals are:

Develop a better predictive model than possible from models based on single independent variables
Investigate the relative individual effects of each predictor variable above and beyond the effects of the other variables
The individual effects of each predictor on the response can be depicted by partial regression lines
The slope of any partial regression line represents the rate of change of that predictor on the response, holding all other predictors constant at their means

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Additive and Multiplicative Models
Additive model — each predictor contributes independently:

EquationLaTeX


\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \ldots + \beta_j x_{ij} + \epsilon_i\]


y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \ldots + \beta_j x_{ij} + \epsilon_i



Multiplicative model — includes an interaction between two predictors:

EquationLaTeX


\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \beta_3 x_{i1} x_{i2} + \epsilon_i\]


y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \beta_3 x_{i1} x_{i2} + \epsilon_i

R Example: Multiple Regression with 2 Predictors
Read in the RNAseq_lip.tsv and examine whether Gene01 and/or Gene02 expression levels influence lipid content.

CodeQuestions



RNAseq_Data <- read.table('RNAseq_lip.tsv', header = TRUE, sep = '\t')

y  <- RNAseq_Data$Lipid_Conc
g1 <- RNAseq_Data$Gene01
g2 <- RNAseq_Data$Gene02

# Multiplicative model (with interaction)
Mult_lm <- lm(y ~ g1 * g2)
summary(Mult_lm)

What are the outcomes from the hypothesis tests?

summary(Add_lm)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Multiple Regression Assumptions
Multiple regression carries all the assumptions of simple regression plus an additional one:

Linearity — the relationship between predictors and response is linear
Normality — residuals are normally distributed
Homogeneity of variance — constant variance of residuals
Independence — observations are independent
No multicollinearity — a predictor variable must not be strongly correlated with the combination of other predictor variables







Multicollinearity


When predictors are highly correlated, coefficient estimates become unstable, standard errors inflate, and interpretation becomes unreliable. Always check for collinearity before interpreting a multiple regression model.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Checking for Multicollinearity


CodeInterpretation



library(car)

# Visual check with scatterplot matrix
scatterplotMatrix(~ var1 + var2 + var3, diag = "boxplot")

# Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
model <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3)
vif(model)

# Tolerance = 1/VIF (values < 0.1 indicate severe collinearity)
1 / vif(model)






VIF Value
Interpretation




1
No collinearity


1–5
Moderate (usually acceptable)


5–10
High (investigate further)


> 10
Severe (remedial action needed)

text:
Bioengineering Example: Scaffold Properties and Tissue Growth

CodeQuestions



# Simulated bioengineering data: predicting tissue growth
# from scaffold porosity, stiffness, and cell seeding density
set.seed(42)
n <- 60

scaffold_data <- data.frame(
  porosity     = runif(n, 40, 90),         # percent porosity
  stiffness    = runif(n, 5, 50),          # kPa
  seeding_dens = runif(n, 1e4, 1e6)        # cells/mL
)
scaffold_data$tissue_growth <- with(scaffold_data,
  0.8 * porosity + 0.3 * stiffness - 0.00001 * seeding_dens +
  0.005 * porosity * stiffness + rnorm(n, 0, 8)
)

# Fit multiple regression
scaffold_lm <- lm(tissue_growth ~ porosity + stiffness + seeding_dens,
                   data = scaffold_data)
summary(scaffold_lm)




Which scaffold properties significantly predict tissue growth?
Does adding the interaction porosity:stiffness improve the model?
What happens to the seeding density coefficient when you remove it?

OutputCodeInterpretation

plot(scaffold_lm)

# Using ggfortify for prettier diagnostics
library(ggfortify)
autoplot(scaffold_lm, which = 1:4) + theme_minimal()

# Cook's distance — identify influential observations
cooks_d <- cooks.distance(scaffold_lm)
plot(cooks_d, type = "h", main = "Cook's Distance",
     ylab = "Cook's Distance", xlab = "Observation")
abline(h = 4 / n, col = "red", lty = 2)




Residuals vs Fitted: look for non-linearity (curved pattern) or heteroscedasticity (funnel shape)
Q-Q Plot: points should follow the diagonal line; deviations indicate non-normality
Scale-Location: check for constant variance (flat trend line)
Residuals vs Leverage: Cook’s distance > 4/n flags influential points

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
The Problem of Model Complexity

How do we decide the complexity of a polynomial: straight line, quadratic, cubic, …?
Which variables should we keep or discard when building a multiple regression model?
How do we select from candidate models representing different biological processes?







Principle of Parsimony


“Models should be pared down until they are minimal and adequate” — Crawley 2007
If two or more models fit the data almost equally well, prefer the simpler model.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Overfitting with Polynomials

The log-likelihood and \(R^2\) always increase with more parameters — but this does not mean the model is better!

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
The Progression of Polynomial Fits





Linear fit






Quadratic fit

text:
Higher-Order Polynomials and Overfitting





Degree 5 polynomial






Degree 10 polynomial



As polynomial degree increases, the model fits the training data ever more closely — but becomes useless for prediction on new data.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Model Selection Criteria








Criterion
Description
Selection Rule




MSresiduals
Mean unexplained variation
Lowest value = best fit


Adjusted R²
Proportion of variance explained, penalized for # terms
Larger = better fit


Mallow’s Cp
Comparison to full model
Lowest value, or closest to p


AIC
Likelihood penalized by number of parameters
Smaller = more parsimonious


BIC
Like AIC but heavier penalty for complexity
Smaller = more parsimonious









Tip


As a rule of thumb, if the difference between two AIC values (ΔAIC) is greater than 2, the lower AIC represents a meaningfully better model.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Mallow’s Cp and All-Subsets Regression


CodeKey Points



library(leaps)

# All subsets regression
all_subsets <- regsubsets(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3 + g4, data = RNAseq_Data)
summary(all_subsets)

# Plot Cp, BIC, adjusted R²
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(all_subsets, scale = "Cp")
plot(all_subsets, scale = "bic")
plot(all_subsets, scale = "adjr2")




For prediction: All models with Cp < p predict about equally well
For explanation: If numerous models fit equally well, it is difficult to deduce which predictor “explains” the response
General caveat: “Regression is not causation” — an experiment is needed for causal explanation

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Nested vs. Non-Nested Models

Nested (reduced vs. full): One model is a special case of the other — can compare with F-test or likelihood ratio test
Non-nested: Models contain different sets of variables — compare with AIC or BIC


CodeInterpretation



# Compare nested models with F-test
model_reduced <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2)
model_full    <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3)
anova(model_reduced, model_full)

# Compare non-nested models with AIC
AIC(model_a, model_b, model_c)
BIC(model_a, model_b, model_c)




F-test p < 0.05 → the fuller model is significantly better
Lower AIC/BIC → more parsimonious model
BIC penalizes complexity more heavily than AIC

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Stepwise Model Selection in R

CodeKey Points



# Start with a full model
full_model <- lm(tissue_growth ~ porosity * stiffness * seeding_dens,
                 data = scaffold_data)

# Forward stepwise selection (start from intercept-only)
null_model <- lm(tissue_growth ~ 1, data = scaffold_data)
forward_model <- step(null_model,
                      scope = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_model),
                      direction = "forward", trace = 1)

# Backward elimination (start from full model)
backward_model <- step(full_model, direction = "backward", trace = 1)

# Both directions
both_model <- step(null_model,
                   scope = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_model),
                   direction = "both", trace = 1)

# Compare final models
AIC(forward_model, backward_model, both_model)
BIC(forward_model, backward_model, both_model)




step() uses AIC by default; add k = log(n) for BIC-based selection
Forward selection can miss important combinations
Backward elimination can fail when p > n
“Both” direction is generally most robust
Stepwise methods can overfit — always validate with cross-validation

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
What is Power?
Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (i.e., detecting a real effect when one exists).

EquationLaTeX


\[\text{Power} \propto \frac{(\text{Effect Size})(\alpha)(\sqrt{n})}{\sigma}\]


\text{Power} \propto \frac{(\text{Effect Size})(\alpha)(\sqrt{n})}{\sigma}




Helps interpret failure to reject the null — was the test underpowered?
Target: typically 80% power (β = 0.20)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Power Overview

Statistical power and Type II error

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Key Components of Power



Component
Description




Effect Size (ES)
Magnitude of difference to detect


Standard Deviation (σ)
Variability within groups


Sample Size (n)
Number of observations


Significance Level (α)
Usually 0.05


Power (1 − β)
Usually 0.80




Key questions in power analysis

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Cohen’s d
Effect size between two group means expressed in standard deviation units:

EquationLaTeX


\[d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{pooled}}\]


d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{pooled}}






d
Interpretation




0.2
Small effect


0.5
Medium effect


0.8
Large effect

Required n per group: 64





library(pwr)

# Calculate required sample size for 80% power

  sig.level = 0.05,

cat("Required n per group:", ceiling(sample_size$n))

})

     xlab = "Effect Size (Cohen's d)", ylab = "Power", ylim = c(0, 1))

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Bootstrap Power Analysis
When parametric assumptions may not hold, use simulation-based power analysis:

CodeKey Points



# Step 1: Simulate true populations
senior <- rpois(5000, lambda = 10)
fresh  <- rpois(5000, lambda = 12)

# Step 2: Draw samples and test
sample_s <- sample(senior, size = 10, replace = FALSE)
sample_f <- sample(fresh, size = 10, replace = FALSE)
t.test(sample_f, sample_s)

# Step 3: Replicate many times
samps_s <- replicate(n = 100, sample(senior, size = 10))
samps_f <- replicate(n = 100, sample(fresh, size = 10))

# Calculate power
tests <- data.frame(result = numeric(100))
for (i in 1:100) {
  tests$result[i] <- t.test(samps_s[, i], samps_f[, i])$p.value
}
power <- sum(tests$result < 0.05) / 100
cat("Estimated power:", power)




This approach works for any distribution (Poisson, skewed, etc.)
Increase the number of replicates (e.g., 1000+) for stable estimates
Can modify sample sizes, effect sizes, or distributions to explore scenarios

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Power Analysis for ANOVA

CodeCohen’s f



library(pwr)

# Parameters for one-way ANOVA
effect_size_anova <- 0.25  # Cohen's f (medium)
alpha_anova <- 0.05
power_anova <- 0.8

# Calculate required sample size per group
sample_size_anova <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = 3,                    # Number of groups
  f = effect_size_anova,
  sig.level = alpha_anova,
  power = power_anova
)$n

cat("Sample Size per group for ANOVA:", ceiling(sample_size_anova))



Cohen’s f measures effect size in ANOVA:



f
Interpretation




0.10
Small effect


0.25
Medium effect


0.40
Large effect



Cohen’s f = √(variance between groups / variance within groups)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Power Example: Bone Scaffold Experiment
A bioengineering lab needs to determine how many bone scaffolds to test to detect a 15% difference in compressive strength between two scaffold designs.

CodeKey Takeaway



# Known from pilot data:
# Mean compressive strength: 50 MPa
# Standard deviation: 8 MPa
# Desired detectable difference: 15% = 7.5 MPa

effect_size_d <- 7.5 / 8  # Cohen's d = 0.94

scaffold_power <- pwr.t.test(
  d = effect_size_d,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80,
  type = "two.sample"
)

cat("Required scaffolds per group:", ceiling(scaffold_power$n))
cat("\nEffect size (Cohen's d):", round(effect_size_d, 2))




With a large effect size (d ≈ 0.94), we need relatively few samples
If the expected difference were only 5% (3.75 MPa, d ≈ 0.47), sample size would roughly quadruple
Always conduct a power analysis before running your experiment

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Power for Factorial ANOVA

CodeTip



library(pwr)

# Power for a 2×3 factorial design
# (e.g., 2 scaffold materials × 3 growth factor concentrations)
pwr.anova.test(
  k = 6,           # Total number of cells (2 × 3)
  f = 0.30,        # Medium-large effect
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)

# For interaction effects specifically:
# Interactions are typically harder to detect
# Use a smaller f value or plan for more samples
pwr.anova.test(
  k = 6,
  f = 0.20,        # Small-medium for interaction
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)



Interactions typically have smaller effect sizes than main effects. Budget extra samples if detecting interactions is important to your study.

gene       <- rna_data$Gene100

# Additive model (no interaction)

summary(model_interaction)
summary(model_additive)




If the interaction term is significant, the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other
If the interaction is not significant, interpret the main effects directly
Always check the interaction first before interpreting main effects

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Fixed vs. Random Effects
Fixed effects:

Groups are predetermined, of direct interest, repeatable
Examples: medical treatments, predetermined doses, habitat types
We want to estimate specific group means

Random effects:

Groups randomly sampled from a larger population
Examples: families, subjects measured repeatedly, blocks, batches
Variance among groups is of interest, not specific group means

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
When to Use Random Effects

Nested sampling designs (individuals within populations)
Subplots within plots
Replicates grouped spatially or temporally (blocks, batches)
Related individuals (families, litters)
Repeated measures on the same subjects

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Random Effects Hypothesis

EquationLaTeX


\[H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0\] \[H_A: \sigma^2_\alpha \neq 0\]


H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0
H_A: \sigma^2_\alpha \neq 0



We are testing whether the variance component for the random effect is zero — i.e., whether there is meaningful variation among the randomly sampled groups.

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Random Effects in R

CodeKey Points



library(nlme)

# Random effect model
micro_model_random_effect <- lme(
  fixed  = Gene202 ~ 1,
  random = ~1 | Geno.Micro,
  data   = stickle_micro
)

summary(micro_model_random_effect)




In R, lm() assumes all effects are fixed
For random effects, use lme() from the nlme package or lmer() from lme4
The ~1 | group syntax specifies a random intercept for each level of group

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Random Effects: Bioengineering Example
Measuring cell viability across multiple wells within multiple plates within multiple experiments:

CodeInterpreting Variance Components



# Simulated hierarchical data: cells → wells → plates → experiments
set.seed(42)
n_exp <- 3; n_plate <- 4; n_well <- 6
experiment <- rep(1:n_exp, each = n_plate * n_well)
plate      <- rep(rep(1:n_plate, each = n_well), n_exp)
well       <- rep(1:n_well, n_exp * n_plate)

# Generate data with variance at each level
exp_effect   <- rnorm(n_exp, 0, 5)[experiment]
plate_effect <- rnorm(n_exp * n_plate, 0, 3)[interaction(experiment, plate)]
viability    <- 75 + exp_effect + plate_effect + rnorm(n_exp * n_plate * n_well, 0, 2)

cell_data <- data.frame(
  viability, experiment = factor(experiment),
  plate = factor(plate), well = factor(well)
)

# Fit nested random effects model
library(nlme)
nested_model <- lme(viability ~ 1,
                    random = ~1 | experiment/plate,
                    data = cell_data)
summary(nested_model)

# Extract variance components
VarCorr(nested_model)



The output from VarCorr() shows:

Experiment variance: variation between experimental runs
Plate-within-experiment variance: variation between plates within a run
Residual variance: well-to-well variation within plates
ICC (Intraclass Correlation) = group variance / total variance

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
Nested Design

Factors are hierarchical within one another
Sources of variance are hierarchical
No interaction terms (in completely nested designs)

Example: Students within classrooms within schools

CodeInterpretation



# Nested ANOVA using aov
model_nested <- aov(y ~ A + B %in% A, data = mydata)

# Using lme for random nested effects
model_nested_random <- lme(y ~ A, random = ~1 | A/B, data = mydata)

summary(model_nested_random)




The %in% notation means “B is nested within A”
The ~1 | A/B random effects specification means “random intercepts for B nested within A”
Nested designs arise when the levels of one factor are unique to each level of another (e.g., specific cell lines unique to each lab)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
What are Repeated Measures?
Measurements taken on the same subjects at multiple:

Time points (longitudinal studies)
Conditions (within-subjects design)
Locations (spatial sampling)

Advantages: Controls for individual differences, requires fewer subjects, more statistical power
Challenge: Observations are not independent — standard ANOVA assumes independence

Sphericity Assumption:

Variances of differences between all pairs of conditions must be equal
Often violated in practice

Mauchly’s Test: Tests the sphericity assumption

p < 0.05 → sphericity is violated → apply correction (Greenhouse-Geisser or Huynh-Feldt)

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10
text:
What is a GLM?
GLMs extend linear models to handle response variables that are not normally distributed. Use when standard linear model assumptions are violated:

Binary response (e.g., survived/died) → logistic regression
Count response (e.g., number of mutations) → Poisson regression

Three components of every GLM:

Random component: probability distribution of the response variable (e.g., binomial, Poisson)
Systematic component: linear combination of predictors (\(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \ldots\))
Link function: connects the random and systematic components

title: Statistics for Bioengineering - Weeks 7–10

Family
Link Function
Use For
Example

identity
